item.title: Displacement-noise-free gravitational-wave detector using quantum tomography of photon orbital angular momentum states
item.description: arXiv:2610.21112v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Gravitational waves (GWs) induce quantum transitions between photon orbital-angular-momentum (OAM) states with amplitudes $\alpha_{\pm}$. Exploiting this effect, we present a displacement-noise-free detection framework that extracts GW information from the OAM Hilbert space. Parametrized quantum state tomography of the GW-induced OAM sidebands enables a single V-shaped detector to resolve all seven wave parameters: the frequency, propagation direction, two polarization amplitudes, and initial phase of each polarization. Direct detection of the sidebands yields a weak signal of approximately $10^{-15}\,\mathrm{W}$. We therefore introduce a stronger reference state $r |0>_{\mathrm{P}}$, with $r=0.01$, to enhance the detected signal. For an arm length of $L=4\,\mathrm{m}$, $N=160$ round trips, a paraxial parameter of $\gamma=0.1$, an incident light power of $P_{\mathrm{BS}}=10\,\mathrm{kW}$, a wavelength of $\lambda_{\mathrm{opt}}=1064\,\mathrm{nm}$, and GW amplitudes of $A=10^{-18}$, we estimate sideband transition amplitudes of $|\alpha_{\pm}|\sim10^{-10}$ and signal powers of order $1\,\mathrm{nW}$, scaling as $P_{\mathrm{BS}}\alpha_{\pm}\propto P_{\mathrm{BS}}ANL\gamma/\lambda_{\mathrm{opt}}$. The shot-noise-limited sensitivity floor is $S^{1/2}_n=1.6\times10^{-20}\,\mathrm{Hz}^{-1/2}$. Because the scheme measures OAM transition amplitudes rather than differential arm lengths, it is intrinsically free from displacement noise and provides a broadband probe of GWs, specifically bridging the $0.1$--$10\,\mathrm{Hz}$ mid-frequency gap.

item.title: Dark Matter Particle Explorer: Ten-Year On-Orbit Performance and Scientific Outcomes
item.description: arXiv:2610.21168v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The Dark Matter Particle Explorer (DAMPE, also known as ``Wukong'') is the first scientific space mission within the framework of the Strategic Pioneer Program on Space Science of the Chinese Academy of Sciences. The main scientific objectives of DAMPE include indirect detection of dark matter, cosmic-ray physics, and high energy gamma-ray astronomy. Thanks to its large geometrical factor and thick imaging calorimeter, DAMPE could effectively detect cosmic-ray electrons (including positrons) and gamma-rays up to 10~TeV, and nuclei up to PeV. Since launched on 17 December 2015 into a Sun-synchronous orbit, DAMPE has been smoothly operating on orbit for more than ten years. Here we present an overview of instrument, on-orbit status, and highlight scientific results of DAMPE, including the measurements of the all-electron energy spectrum and the spectra of protons and other nuclei, and high energy gamma-ray line search.
item.dc:creator: Jian-Hua Guo, Chuan Yue, Yun-Long Zhang, Yi-Zhong Fan, Jin Chang

item.title: A machine-learning-driven dataset of 144,111 polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon infrared spectra for interpreting aromatic infrared bands
item.description: arXiv:2610.21205v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The interpretation of interstellar aromatic infrared bands (AIBs) relies on reference spectral libraries, but the chemical space covered by existing databases remains incomplete relative to the vast structural diversity of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) expected in the interstellar medium. We present a large-scale, high-throughput PAH infrared (IR) spectral database that complements existing reference libraries by providing significantly more continuous coverage of the PAH chemical space for small to medium-sized PAHs. We used a machine-learning double-harmonic (ML-DH) framework that integrates neural network force fields with electronic dipole models. This framework achieves quantum-chemical accuracy at a fraction of the computational cost. It has been validated against independent density functional theory calculations and benchmark spectral databases. The resulting dataset comprises 144,111 IR spectra for 48,037 closed-shell, even-carbon benzenoid PAH structures across neutral, cationic, and anionic charge states, complete with per-spectrum uncertainty estimates. The spectral library, optimized geometries, and model code are publicly available. They can be used to complement existing libraries for interpreting and modeling JWST AIB observations and those from future IR missions.

item.title: Polarization Properties of Thomson-Scattering Triaxial Ellipsoids
item.description: arXiv:2610.21499v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Polarimetry is a powerful tool for constraining the geometry of distant astrophysical objects. Continuum polarization induced by Thomson scattering can probe the photospheric geometry of transients and provide insight into their explosion mechanisms. We systematically study continuum polarization from spheroids over a broader range of deformations and viewing angles than considered previously, and generalize the calculation to triaxial ellipsoids. We find that strongly deformed spheroids exhibit a non-monotonic dependence of polarization on viewing angle, a behavior overlooked in previous studies. Triaxial ellipsoids show more diverse polarization signatures, but their qualitative behavior can be understood from the area of surface elements viewed nearly edge-on, where the local polarization is strongest. Our results provide a simple physical understanding of the dependence of polarization on photospheric geometry and help constrain the geometry of astrophysical transients through polarimetric observations. The computational results of this study will be made publicly available for use in future research.

item.title: WALTzER: Wide-band Atmospheric Laboratory for Transiting Exoplanet Research
item.description: arXiv:2610.21705v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Understanding the origin and evolution of planetary atmospheres, and the connection between their lower and upper atmospheric layers, remains a fundamental challenge in exoplanet science. Addressing these questions requires observations spanning a broad wavelength range, from the ultraviolet to the near-infrared, together with the ability to simultaneously characterise planetary and stellar variability. The Wide-band Atmospheric Laboratory for Transiting Exoplanet Research (WALTzER) is an ESA F3 mission candidate designed to address this need through simultaneous low-resolution spectroscopy and high-precision photometry of transiting exoplanets. WALTzER covers simultaneously the near-ultraviolet (NUV: 240--325 nm) and visible (VIS: 450--820 nm) bands with two medium resolution spectrographs and the near-infrared (NIR: 900--1700 nm) range with a broadband photometer. We outline the main science drivers and present the mission concept and instrument design. WALTzER's broad, simultaneous wavelength coverage enables the detection and characterisation of the atmospheres of more than 30 gas-rich exoplanets and provides data relevant for a broad range of Solar System and Galactic astrophysics science cases. The payload consists of a 35 cm Cassegrain telescope feeding three co-aligned channels (i.e. NUV, VIS, NIR), sharing a common optical train to minimise instrumental systematics, while maximising observational efficiency.

item.title: Time-reversible timestepping in many-body planetary systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.22007v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Simulating chaotic planetary system evolution requires resolving small time-scales due to close encounters, scattering, collisions, and more. Simulations typically assign fixed timesteps to all particles, however, which is inefficient and wastes compute resources in a chaotically evolving system; moreover, it may under-resolve the simulation. Hybrid methods are a blunt tool for resolving small time-scales as they do not allow for fine-grained adaptation. Assigning individual timesteps, which vary in time, to planetary bodies usually violates desirable properties such as symplecticity and reversibility. In this work, we develop an "almost" exactly time-reversible direct $N$-body integrator, MTR, in which each pair of planets gets its own timestep, which itself can vary as the system evolves. In contrast to our previous work, we achieve this adaptation on the fly, independent of a global timestep. We provide a C version of the code and test it on several problems, demonstrating no energy error drift, as expected of a reversible method. At large particle numbers, up to $N = 975$, we compare against the state-of-the-art GPLUM code, which we can use in direct Hermite mode (for which it is not optimized) or tree mode (for which it is). MTR provides a speedup of up to two orders of magnitude compared to the Hermite mode, while agreeing with the distribution of orbits. In our default configuration, MTR's speed matches or improves on the tree mode's speed, by up to an order magnitude, despite the tree mode's faster and approximate force calculation.

item.title: The Radius-Luminosity Relationship for Active Galactic Nuclei with Hierarchical Bayesian Reverberation Mapping
item.description: arXiv:2610.22096v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reverberation mapping of active galactic nuclei uses the time taken for variability to travel through the system as a measure of system size, with this size being used to inform estimates of the mass of the central black hole, a technique that has graduated to an industrial-scale effort in recent decades. Such large target-count, multi-year surveys have been consistently undercut by poor light curve quality and the aliasing problems of seasonal observations. These impacts compound with statistical approaches that are not consistent between works and sometimes combine inconsistent statistical frameworks. Here, we present a new end-to-end Bayesian framework for fitting lags at scale in large surveys, simultaneous with the fitting of population models such as the radius-luminosity relation, and formulated in a numerically tractable way. This procedure is a statistically and numerically robust generalisation of the stacking and quality cut procedures of past works, fully marginalising over data uncertainty and data quality. Our approach remains numerically stable when scaling to larger surveys, and can act as a basis for any Bayesian population modelling of large sets of AGN time series observations. Applied to the OzDES sample, we demonstrate that this new approach yields more than double the constraining power on population-level properties like the R-L relationship, and an order-of-magnitude increase in the number of recovered lags and masses. With this method, we go from 24 high quality lag recoveries with traditional methods to a new effective sample size of ~297, all while being robust against random chance false positive measurements.

item.title: A New Method for Constraining 3D Exoplanet Atmospheres: Application to WASP-94A b's Panchromatic Spectrum
item.description: arXiv:2610.22271v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A growing number of transiting exoplanets exhibit spectroscopic evidence that their leading and trailing limbs differ. Interpreting these observations is now the limiting step. The standard approach of fitting limb-resolved transit depths results in highly anti-correlated transit depths, and treating them as independent measurements can result in strongly biased ($3\sigma$) retrieved molecular abundances. We present an inference framework that avoids these correlations by using the temporal signature of limb asymmetry instead. This wavelength-dependent shift in mid-transit time, or `time-shift spectrum', carries the limb-asymmetry information, is measurable from existing light curves with a spherically symmetric transit model, and is uncorrelated with the spherically-averaged transit depth. Simultaneously fitting the resulting transmission and time-shift spectrum with an independent atmospheric column for each limb enables the retrieval of limb-resolved properties from two independent measurements. We demonstrate that this approach reduces the mean squared error on the retrieved molecular abundances by factors of $\sim30-50$ relative to next best of the alternative approaches currently adopted in the field, and improves retrieved abundance precision by $\sim3-6\times$. We apply the framework to WASP-94A b and present its panchromatic limb-resolved spectrum, spanning 0.8-5~$\mu$m and combining NIRISS/SOSS and NIRSpec/G395H observations. The planet's morning limb remains aerosol-obscured across this entire range, while its evening limb constrains the abundances of H$_2$O, CO$_2$, CO, and H$_2$S. We measure a limb-to-limb temperature difference of $415\pm58$~K at 1~mbar. This limb-resolved analysis finds [M/H]=+0.32$^{+0.11}_{-0.11}$ and C/O=0.724$^{+0.013}_{-0.013}$, consistent with the host star.

item.title: Identifying deformed exoplanets with JWST and Ariel: A target selection metric for phase curve observations
item.description: arXiv:2610.22338v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The shape of an exoplanet encodes fundamental information about its internal structure. For close-in giant planets, strong stellar tidal forces induce measurable deformations that can be probed through high-precision photometry. These deformations are quantified by the fluid Love numbers, which characterise a planet's response to external perturbations and are directly linked to its internal density distribution. In this work, we assess the potential of JWST and the future Ariel mission to constrain the Love numbers of hot Jupiters through full-orbit phase curve observations. To identify the most promising targets for this science case, we introduce a new detection metric, the deformation metric (D), which combines the expected deformation amplitude with the anticipated photometric signal-to-noise ratio. We apply this metric to the Ariel target list and identify WASP-33 b, WASP-76 b, and HAT-P-32 b as the three most favourable targets that currently lack Love number measurements. Using WASP-76 b as a benchmark case, we perform end-to-end retrieval simulations and show that a single continuous JWST phase curve observation can constrain the Love number $h_{2f}$ to a precision of $\sigma_{h_2f} \approx 0.09$, while a single Ariel visit could achieve $\sigma_{h_{2f}} \approx 0.18$. Such precision is likely sufficient for Love number measurements to provide meaningful constraints on planetary interior models and to distinguish between competing interior-structure scenarios, opening a new observational avenue for probing the deep interiors of exoplanets.

item.title: Singles in Disguise: Kepler's Low-SNR Single-Transiting Systems as Incompletely Detected Multis
item.description: arXiv:2610.22349v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: NASA's Kepler mission found more systems with one transiting planet (``singles'') than expected from those with several (``multis''). This excess was first taken as evidence for a Kepler dichotomy -- a second population of intrinsically single or highly inclined systems -- but later work argued that selection effects acting on a single population can reproduce it. Singles also show a puzzling excess of low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) detections relative to multis. The question arises whether this excess reflects false positives, a selection effect, or an inherent population difference. Here we show, using the ExoMOD population synthesis model and the Kepler DR25 catalog, that multis drawn from the same parent population as singles have shorter mean orbital periods, and thus higher-SNR detections on average. Detecting several planets in one system favors compact architectures, so long-period, low-SNR detections are preferentially cataloged as singles, most of them intrinsically multi-planet systems whose other planets went undetected. The low-SNR excess of singles therefore requires neither false positives nor a Kepler dichotomy but rather only the geometry and period sensitivity of transit detection.

item.title: Using 23 Years of ACS/SBC Data to Understand Backgrounds: Significant Reductions in Expected Background Levels
item.description: arXiv:2601.02551v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We have used 23 years of Hubble Space Telescope ACS/SBC data to study what background levels are encountered in practice and how much they vary. The backgrounds vary considerably, with F115LP, F122M, F125LP, PR110L, and PR130L all showing over an order of magnitude of variation in background between observations, apparently due to changes in airglow. The F150LP and F165LP filters, which are dominated by dark rate, not airglow, exhibit a far smaller variation in backgrounds. For the filters where the background is generally dominated by airglow, the backgrounds measured from the data are significantly lower than what the ETC predicts (as of ETC v33.2). The ETC predictions for `average' airglow are greater than the median of our measured background values by factors of 2.51, 2.64, 105, and 3.64, for F115LP, F122M, F125LP, and F140LP, respectively. A preliminary analysis suggests this could be due to certain OI airglow lines usually being fainter than expected by the ETC. With reduced reduced background levels, the shorter-wavelength SBC filters can conduct background-limited observations much more rapidly than had previously been expected. As of ETC v34.1, a new option will be included for SBC calculations, allowing users to employ empirical background percentiles to estimate required exposure times.
item.dc:creator: Christopher. J. R. Clark, Roberto J. Avila, Alyssa M. Guzman, Norman A. Grogin

item.title: Using 23 Years of ACS/SBC Data to Understand Backgrounds: Explaining & Predicting Background Variations
item.description: arXiv:2601.09682v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recent analysis of 23 years of Hubble Space Telescope ACS/SBC data has shown that background levels can vary considerably between observations, with most filters showing over an order of magnitude variation. For the shorter-wavelength filters, the background is understood to be dominated by airglow; however, what precisely drives background variations is not well constrained for any filter. Here, we explore the causes of the background variation. Using over 8,000 archival SBC observations, we developed a machine learning model that can accurately predict the background for an observation, based upon a set of 23 observational parameters. This model indicates that, depending on filter, the SBC background is generally dominated by Solar elevation, Solar separation angle, Earth limb angle of observation, SBC temperature, and target Galactic latitude.
item.dc:creator: Christopher J. R. Clark, Roberto J. Avila, Alyssa M. Guzman, Norman A. Grogin

item.title: Co-design of ground-based gravitational wave detector networks
item.description: arXiv:2607.27254v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Discussions around the design philosophy and location of the next generation of ground-based gravitational wave detectors are still underway. In this context, we propose IfoScout, an innovative methodology for detector co-design based on state-of-the-art machine-learning (ML) techniques. As a simple demonstration, we present a two-stage simulation of a network of fictional L-shaped interferometers whose sensitivity is optimized within physical and geographical constraints, indirectly resulting in reducing the costs. To achieve this, we gather publicly available data for two token locations and establish the length and orientation with reinforcement learning (RL). Next, we optimize the internal detector parameters related to cavity stability to achieve the best possible sensitivity by means of differential programming (DP). We make the case that pipelines such as IfoScout could have a positive impact on the final design of new generation detectors (e.g. the Einstein Telescope, the Cosmic Explorer, etc.), given precise data and detailed, realistic simulations of the interferometers.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Lanchares, Lysiane Mornas, Luigi Toffolatti, Pietro Vischia

item.title: Beyond the BLUE I: the advantage ceiling - how much can any estimator beat the matched filter in mm/submm survey data?
item.description: arXiv:2609.10475v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Papers claiming that convolutional neural networks outperform the matched filter are now common in astronomy. Since that filter is the best linear unbiased estimator (BLUE) for any noise of given covariance, and the minimum-variance unbiased estimator under Gaussian noise, such a claim requires that the noise covariance varies from image to image or the noise is non-Gaussian. We introduce the advantage ceiling eta >= 1, which quantifies both cases: the Fisher information for the amplitude in units of the matched filter's, computable from noise-only simulations before any network is trained, and a bound on the variance of any estimator unbiased at each true amplitude. We compute eta for a suite of millimeter/submillimeter survey noise models and for compact and extended source templates, using a variational score-matching ladder whose rungs are estimator classes of increasing statistical order, from linear to convolutional. With an instrumental white-noise floor, Gaussian noise returns eta = 0.94-1.06 (+-0.04); covariance mixtures give exact ceilings of 10.2 (spectral tilt, extended source), 2.1 (leaked components) and 1.1-1.8 otherwise; residual artifacts give eta <= 1.09. Source confusion gives the largest advantage, eta >= 3.8 (extended) and >= 2.4 (compact). Three unmodelled channels - a zeroed DC mode, a missing white floor and floating-point rounding - can manufacture spurious advantages of up to two orders of magnitude. A ResNet regressor is 6-15% less efficient than the matched filter on Gaussian noise once prior shrinkage is divided out, and realizes a factor 1.8 of the 10.2 available on the spectral-tilt mixture; a companion paper tests such regressors against these ceilings.
item.dc:creator: Kaustuv Basu

item.title: The optical high-resolution spectral archive of the HERMES spectrograph mounted on the 1.2m Mercator telescope
item.description: arXiv:2609.22029v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Context. The HERMES spectrograph is a high-resolution, fibre-fed optical spectrograph of the 1.2m Mercator telescope operated from the Roque de los Muchachos observatory in Spain. HERMES started its scientific operations in June 2009 and has been the workhorse instrument since then. Regular instrument updates have been crucial. They have helped to ensure the continued provision of high-quality spectra. This will continue both now and in the future. Aims. With this contribution we review over 16 years of HERMES operations and we launch and introduce the archive to the interna- tional community at large. We describe the overall performances of the HERMES spectrograph and list the most important instrument upgrades since the start of the operations. We release about 150 000 high-resolution spectra to the community and describe global properties of the datarelease. We use a standard propriety period of 1 year with some exceptions. Methods. We used the German Astrophysical Virtual Observatory (GAVO) DaCHS platform to present the archive in a Virtual Ob- servatory (VO) compatible form with both an access via a dedicated webinterface, and via VO-compliant tools like PyVO, TOPCAT, Aladin etc. We illustrate the use in several worked-out examples to search and download the fully wavelength-calibrated, cosmic- cleaned and barycentric corrected 1D spectra. Results. With this contribution we provide the needed information of the data product and offer a reference paper for the users of the HERMES archive.

item.title: XuYi Interferometer Observation Simulator
item.description: arXiv:2610.07042v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The XuYi Interferometer is the first Chinese long-baseline optical interferometer currently under development by the National Institute of Astronomical Optics and Technology (NIAOT) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences. In preparation for future scientific operations, we developed the XuYi Interferometer Observation Simulator (XIOS), a lightweight MATLAB-based software package designed to assist observers in planning interferometric observations. The simulator combines target observability calculations, interferometric baseline geometry, delay-line constraints, (u,v)-coverage prediction, and visibility estimation into a single graphical user interface. It incorporates astronomical routines from the MAAT toolbox and adopts visualization concepts inspired by ASPRO2. The software allows users to evaluate observing opportunities, predict interferometric performances, and generate realistic observing configurations before telescope operations. We present the architecture of the simulator, its principal modules, and representative simulation results obtained for the current three-telescope XuYi interferometric configuration operating in the near-infrared H band.
